chief_complaint: fatigue, dyspnea, orthopnea, and blowing systolic murmur
hpi_details: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with fatigue, dyspnea, orthopnea, and blowing systolic murmur. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks his severe breathlessness and fatigue are from a lingering chest cold that settled in his lungs from working long hours.
concerns: He is worried he will have to give up playing soccer on the weekends and won't be able to keep up with his active job.
expectations: He hopes the doctor will prescribe an inhaler or strong decongestant so he can breathe easily and sleep flat in bed again.

investigation_events.title: Transthoracic echocardiogram
investigation_events.availability_message: The transthoracic echocardiogram report is now available.

results.value: Severe primary mitral regurgitation from posterior leaflet prolapse; effective regurgitant orifice 0.48 cm2; regurgitant volume 68 mL; LVEF 60%

clinical_knowledge.topic: Severe Mitral Regurgitation evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Severe Mitral Regurgitation is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes echocardiographic definition of mitral-regurgitation severity and mechanism, followed by valve-team assessment when severe disease is confirmed, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Severe Mitral Regurgitation.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Aortic stenosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Sudden worsening — possible chordae rupture.
management_principles: Plan for suspected mitral regurgitation: obtain echocardiography to establish severity and mechanism; refer confirmed severe disease for valve-team assessment
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of fatigue, dyspnea, orthopnea, and blowing systolic murmur. HPI: mitral valve prolapse/flail leaflet.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Severe Mitral Regurgitation.
reference_soap.assessment: Mitral regurgitation is suspected from the symptoms and blowing systolic murmur; echocardiography is required to establish severity and mechanism.
reference_soap.plan: Plan for suspected mitral regurgitation: obtain echocardiography to establish severity and mechanism; refer confirmed severe disease for valve-team assessment. Repair is preferred when durable repair is feasible, while replacement is selected for appropriate anatomy or mechanism. Seek urgent evaluation for sudden deterioration. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Severe Mitral Regurgitation
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Severe Mitral Regurgitation
Implement evidence-based management plan: Echocardiogram, refer for mitral valve repair or replacement

teaching.one_liner: A flail or prolapsing mitral valve leaflet allows significant backward blood flow, causing fatigue, breathlessness, and orthopnea with a blowing systolic murmur.

history.answer: I've been feeling unusually tired lately, and whenever I lie flat in bed, I get so short of breath that I have to prop myself up.
It started about three or four weeks ago and has been gradually getting worse.
I get winded just climbing one flight of stairs or walking up a slight incline, whereas I used to run without any problem.
The shortness of breath has been steadily progressing, rather than coming and going in sudden attacks.
I have to stack two or three pillows under my head to sleep, and I woke up twice last week gasping for air and had to sit by the window.
It gets noticeably worse whenever I exert myself or lie flat, and it settles down when I sit upright and rest.
No, I haven't heard any wheezing or whistling sounds when I breathe.
I have a dry cough that pops up when I lie down, but I don't have any phlegm, chills, or fever.
No, I haven't had any squeezing chest pain or sharp pain when taking a deep breath.
My heart feels like it pounds rapidly whenever I walk upstairs, but I have not had dizziness or blackouts.
No, I have never coughed up blood.
I noticed my socks leaving deep indentations around my ankles by evening, but my body weight has stayed about the same.
No, neither leg is swollen or tender, and I haven't had any surgeries or long-distance flights recently.
I feel drained and worn out by mid-afternoon even after a full night of rest, but I haven't seen any pale skin or dark stools.
No, my hands and mouth do not tingle, and I don't feel like this is caused by hyperventilation or stress.
A doctor during a routine college health checkup mentioned I had a slight heart murmur or floppy valve, but told me it was harmless back then.
I have never had asthma, COPD, heart attacks, or heart failure, and I've never used an inhaler.
I work at a desk in an office, so I am not exposed to dust, chemicals, mold, or birds.
No, I don't take beta-blockers, pain relievers like ibuprofen, or any other regular medications.
I thought I just picked up a lingering chest cold or bad flu that settled into my lungs from working long hours.
I'm really worried this means I won't be able to play soccer anymore or keep up with my physically demanding job.
I have always been healthy and have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure or diabetes.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter medicines, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications or food.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products.
I only drink one or two glasses of beer socially on weekends.
I work as an office administrator and live in an apartment with my partner.
Both of my parents are healthy, and there is no history of early heart disease or sudden cardiac death in my family.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, pulse rate 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6°C, oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
Alert and mildly tachypneic at rest without accessory muscle use; no perioral cyanosis or digital clubbing.
Palpebral conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are non-icteric.
Mildly elevated jugular venous pressure estimated at approximately 4 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees.
Percussion note is resonant symmetrically across all lung fields.
Fine end-inspiratory crackles are audible at both lung bases without wheezes or rhonchi.
Grade 3/6 high-pitched blowing holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex with radiation to the left axilla, along with an audible third heart sound.
Trace to 1+ bilateral pitting edema noted over the pretibial regions and ankles.
Both calves are symmetric without swelling, localized tenderness, warmth, or palpable cords.
